cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/0/: Meals, prayers and the breaking of bread

Believers met in homes on the first day of the week for teaching, prayer and a shared meal that included the Lord's Supper (Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 11). Jewish believers in Jerusalem also continued to frequent the Temple until 70. Baptism, usually by immersion 'in the name of Jesus' or of Father, Son and Spirit, marked entry.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/1/: Worship inherited the synagogue's chanting of psalms, and early Christological hymns are probably embedded in Paul's letters (Philippians 2:6–11; Colossians 1:15–20). Singing was unaccompanied; Paul urges believers to sing 'psalms, hymns and spiritual songs' (Ephesians 5:19).
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/2/: There were no church buildings: congregations met in the homes of patrons such as Lydia, Prisca and Aquila, Philemon and Nympha. A wealthy villa's dining room might hold thirty to forty people, so a city's church was a network of household assemblies.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/3/: No Christian art survives from the first century. Inheriting the Jewish prohibition of images, believers expressed faith through words, gestures and symbols such as baptismal water and bread; visual art appears only in the late second century.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/4/: There were no monasteries, but itinerant apostles and prophets renounced home and possessions, and Paul commended celibacy for undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7). Widows devoted to prayer formed a recognised group (1 Timothy 5).
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/5/: Christians gathered on 'the first day of the week', the day of resurrection, which came to be called the Lord's Day (Revelation 1:10). Jewish believers kept the Sabbath and festivals; an annual Pascha commemorating Christ's death and resurrection grew out of Passover.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/6/: Women were among Jesus' disciples and the first witnesses of the resurrection. Paul greets female co-workers — Phoebe the deacon, Prisca, Junia 'prominent among the apostles' — and women prophesied in worship; how far other texts restrict their roles is debated across traditions.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/7/: Teaching passed orally through apostles, teachers and catechesis, and through letters read aloud in assemblies. The Jewish Scriptures in Greek (the Septuagint) were the church's Bible; the Gospels were written in the latter half of the century.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/8/: The movement spread along synagogue networks and Roman roads to Antioch, Asia Minor, Greece and Rome, and by tradition to Alexandria, Edessa and India. By 100 there were perhaps 7,000–10,000 Christians, mostly urban.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/9/: Believers faced synagogue discipline, mob violence and local magistrates; Stephen and James son of Zebedee were killed in Jerusalem. Nero's persecution in 64 was the first by Roman authority, and Revelation reflects pressure from the imperial cult in Asia.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/10: The earliest believers were Jews who saw Jesus as Israel's Messiah; debate over Gentile inclusion was an intra-Jewish argument. After 70 the paths of the rabbinic movement and the increasingly Gentile church gradually diverged, though the 'parting of the ways' was long and uneven.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/11: Before Islam: paganism and the imperial cult

Islam had not yet arisen. Christians lived among Greco-Roman polytheism, mystery cults and the cult of the emperor, which they refused to join; in Parthian Mesopotamia they encountered Zoroastrian and Babylonian traditions.
cultures/culture-apostolic-age/panels/12: Christians had no legal recognition and were at first regarded as a Jewish sect. New Testament writers urge prayer for and submission to rulers (Romans 13; 1 Peter 2) while Revelation portrays imperial Rome as a beast — the beginning of a lasting tension.
cultures/culture-apostolic-fathers/panel: Eucharist and baptism ordered

The Didache and Justin Martyr describe Sunday gatherings with Scripture readings, a sermon by the presider, prayers, the kiss of peace and the Eucharist taken to the absent by deacons. Baptism followed fasting and instruction; the bishop increasingly presided.
Hymns to Christ
Pliny reports Christians singing 'a hymn to Christ as to a god' at dawn. The Odes of Solomon, a Syriac or Greek hymnbook of the early second century, show a lyrical Christianity in the East.
Homes and meeting halls
Christians still met in private houses and rented halls; Justin says he taught 'above the baths of Myrtinus' in Rome. Burial grounds owned by Christian families foreshadowed the catacombs.
First symbols
Simple symbols appear: the fish (ichthys), anchor, dove and Good Shepherd, often borrowed from pagan art and given Christian meaning. Clement of Alexandria advises suitable images for signet rings.
Ascetics and virgins

Dedicated virgins and continent men lived ascetic lives within congregations. In Syria an ideal of celibate 'sons and daughters of the covenant' was strong, and Tatian's circle (Encratites) required celibacy of all believers.
Easter and martyrs' days

Annual Pascha was universal, but Asia kept it on 14 Nisan while Rome kept Sunday, provoking the Quartodeciman controversy. Smyrna began commemorating Polycarp's 'birthday' into heaven, the origin of saints' days.
Martyrs, prophetesses and widows

Women led in Montanist prophecy and died alongside men at Lyon (Blandina). Orders of widows and virgins were recognised, while some writers increasingly restricted women's teaching as office became more structured.
Apologists and schools

Educated converts like Justin and Athenagoras wrote apologies addressed to emperors, and teachers ran philosophical schools in Rome and Alexandria. Catechumens received instruction lasting up to three years.
Through the cities of the empire and beyond

Christianity reached Gaul, North Africa and Upper Egypt, while Syriac-speaking Christianity grew around Edessa and Adiabene beyond the Roman frontier. Merchants, slaves and soldiers spread the faith more than professional missionaries.
Illegal but rarely hunted

Under Trajan's policy Christians were not sought out but, if accused and obstinate, were executed. Local pogroms killed Polycarp (Smyrna), the martyrs of Lyon and the Scillitans; rumours of cannibalism and incest were common.
Rival claims to Israel's Scriptures

Justin's Dialogue with Trypho reflects real debate with Jews over messianic prophecy. After the Bar Kokhba revolt, separation hardened; Melito of Sardis' Peri Pascha voiced the charge of 'deicide' that later fed Christian anti-Judaism.
Before Islam: paganism and philosophy
Islam had not yet arisen. Christians debated pagan critics such as Celsus and Lucian, and engaged Platonism and Stoicism; Gnostic and Marcionite groups were rival forms of Christianity.
Loyal subjects, not worshippers
Apologists insisted Christians prayed for emperors and paid taxes but could not sacrifice to them. The church had no legal status, though it owned property informally through members.
cultures/culture-persecution-early-theol: Liturgy takes shape

The Apostolic Tradition attributed to Hippolytus preserves a eucharistic prayer and a demanding catechumenate culminating in Easter baptism. Church orders like the Syriac Didascalia regulate seating, ministry and penance; public penance for serious sins developed after the persecutions.
Psalmody and early hymns
The Oxyrhynchus hymn (late 3rd century) is the earliest Christian hymn with musical notation. Syriac Christians sang Bardaisan's hymns, which Ephrem later countered with orthodox ones.
Catacombs and first church buildings

Roman Christians buried their dead in underground catacombs such as that of Callixtus, where martyrs were venerated. Converted houses like Dura-Europos and, by 300, purpose-built halls (Nicomedia's church was visible from the palace) appeared.
Catacomb frescoes

Paintings show Jonah, Daniel, Noah, the raising of Lazarus, the Good Shepherd and orants (praying figures) — images of deliverance and resurrection. Dura's baptistery and its neighbouring synagogue with biblical murals show shared Jewish and Christian visual culture.
Into the desert
Around 270 Antony withdrew into the Egyptian desert, and solitaries gathered around holy men. Syriac 'covenanters' (bnay qyama) lived consecrated celibate lives in local churches.
Lent, Easter and Pentecost
A pre-Easter fast was lengthening toward forty days, and the fifty days of Easter ended at Pentecost. The Coptic 'Era of the Martyrs' calendar counts years from Diocletian's accession in 284.
Martyrs and deaconesses
Perpetua's prison diary is the earliest Christian woman's text. The Didascalia describes deaconesses who assisted at women's baptisms and visited women in their homes.
Origen and the school of Caesarea

Origen's curriculum at Caesarea moved from logic and physics to ethics and theology, culminating in Scripture. Christians debated whether pagan learning was 'spoils of Egypt' or dangerous; Tertullian asked 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?'.
A growing minority

By 300 perhaps 5–10% of the empire was Christian, with strongholds in Asia Minor, North Africa and Egypt, where Coptic translation reached villages. Armenia became the first Christian kingdom, and Roman deportees strengthened the church in Persia.
Empire-wide persecution

Decius (250) demanded universal sacrifice, Valerian (257–58) targeted clergy and property, and Diocletian's Great Persecution (303–311) destroyed churches and Scriptures. Thousands died, and the question of lapsed Christians and traditores split churches.
Adversus Judaeos and coexistence

Tertullian and Cyprian wrote treatises 'Against the Jews', while in daily life Christians and Jews in cities like Antioch and Dura lived side by side and some Christians attended synagogue. Origen consulted Jewish scholars for the Hexapla.
Before Islam: Manichaeism and Zoroastrianism

Islam had not yet arisen. In Persia the Zoroastrian Sasanian state and the new Manichaean religion (Mani d. 276) competed with Christianity; in the Roman world Neoplatonism, led by Plotinus and Porphyry, offered a pagan intellectual alternative.
From persecution to toleration

Periods of peace (260–303) allowed bishops to own property openly, but the state could still demand sacrifice. Galerius' deathbed edict of 311 grudgingly tolerated Christians, preparing for Constantine.
cultures/culture-imperial-church/panels/: Public liturgy

Worship moved into great basilicas with processions, vestments, incense and lamps. Liturgical families formed — the Antiochene (St James, St Basil, St John Chrysostom), Alexandrian (St Mark), Roman, Gallican and East Syriac (Addai and Mari) — and Egeria's diary describes Jerusalem's Holy Week.
Antiphonal psalmody and Ephrem's hymns

Ambrose introduced antiphonal hymn-singing in Milan, and his metrical hymns became models. In the Syriac church Ephrem's madrashe were sung by women's choirs; Arians and Nicenes competed with processional hymns in Constantinople.
The basilica

Constantine built monumental basilicas — the Lateran, St Peter's, the Holy Sepulchre, Bethlehem's Nativity — on the plan of a Roman hall with nave, aisles and apse. Martyria and baptisteries followed; in Aksum, Ezana built early stone churches.
Mosaics and the image of Christ

Apse mosaics like Santa Pudenziana in Rome (c. 400) show Christ enthroned as teacher among the apostles. The Chi-Rho monogram adorned shields and coins; some, like Eusebius, doubted the propriety of images of Christ.
Desert fathers and mothers

Pachomius organised communal monasteries; the Desert Fathers and Mothers of Scetis and Nitria gave rise to the Sayings tradition; Basil wrote monastic rules; Martin of Tours and John Cassian brought monasticism to Gaul. Syrian stylites, beginning with Simeon (c. 423), lived atop pillars.
Christmas and Epiphany

Rome celebrated Christ's nativity on 25 December by 336, while the East kept 6 January (Epiphany); the Armenian church still celebrates the Nativity on 6 January. Nicaea set Easter on the Sunday after the spring full moon, and Lent became a forty-day fast.
Ascetic women and patrons
Women like Macrina, Olympias, Melania the Elder and Paula founded monasteries and funded scholarship; Egeria wrote a pilgrim diary. The empress Helena's pilgrimage made holy-land devotion popular.
Fathers of the Church

Bishops trained in classical rhetoric — the Cappadocians, Chrysostom, Augustine, Jerome — produced the classic literature of patristic theology. The School of Edessa taught Syriac theology, and Mesrop's Armenian alphabet launched a vernacular literature.
Beyond the empire
Frumentius evangelised Aksum, Nino Georgia, Ulfilas the Goths (as Homoians), Patrick Ireland. Christians spread in Arabia (Najran) and along the Persian Gulf, and the Persian church organised in 410.
Persecution in Persia

Roman persecution ended, but Shapur II's forty-year persecution of Persian Christians after 340 produced many martyrs. Within the empire Christians now persecuted pagans, Jews and heretics; Donatists and Nicene and Arian factions also suffered under rival regimes.
Imperial Christianity and the synagogue

Imperial laws restricted Jewish proselytism and synagogue building, and Chrysostom's sermons in Antioch voiced harsh polemic. Augustine argued Jews should be preserved as witnesses to Scripture, a doctrine that both protected and marginalised Jewish communities in the West.
Before Islam: the end of official paganism

Islam had not yet arisen. Theodosius banned pagan sacrifice (391–392); temples were closed or destroyed, such as the Serapeum of Alexandria (391), and Hypatia's murder (415) became a symbol of Christian violence. In Persia, Zoroastrian clergy pressed for persecution.
Christian emperors

Emperors convened councils, enforced orthodoxy and granted clergy legal privileges. Ambrose's confrontation with Theodosius and Augustine's City of God articulated limits to imperial power, foreshadowing distinct Western and Byzantine visions.
